opus-5.5.text:
I'd say it's definitely not solved, although I understand why people might get that impression. Over the last few years we've seen really impressive demos: quadrupeds doing parkour, climbing over boxes, jumping gaps, walking through forests and up stairs. If you only watch the videos, it can look like we're done.

But when you look closer, a lot of those results work in fairly controlled conditions, or the robot has been trained for a specific set of obstacles. The hard part is the long tail. Real environments have things like reflective surfaces, transparent glass, thin poles, tall grass that looks solid to a depth camera but isn't, snow, mud, and bad lighting. Perception systems still struggle with a lot of that, and the policy has to decide how much to trust what it sees versus what it feels through its legs.

There's also the gap between blind locomotion and vision-based locomotion. Blind locomotion, where the robot only uses proprioception, is now very robust. With reinforcement learning in simulation and sim-to-real transfer, you can get controllers that handle almost any terrain reactively. Once you add vision, though, you introduce a whole new sim-to-real gap. Simulating depth sensors or cameras realistically, with the right noise, artifacts and failure modes, is much harder than simulating joint encoders. So getting a policy that uses vision robustly, and degrades gracefully when the vision is wrong, is still an open research question.

And then there's the bigger picture. Locomotion by itself isn't really the end goal. You want the robot to navigate, to understand where it's going, to interact with the world, maybe do loco-manipulation. Combining agile, perceptive locomotion with higher-level reasoning and planning in a single system that works reliably for hours in an unknown environment, without a human babysitting it, is something nobody has fully cracked yet.

So my answer is that we've made huge progress, and certain sub-problems are close to solved, but robust, general-purpose vision-based locomotion in the wild is still very much an active area. That's what makes it exciting to work on.

r001.rationale: The response discusses locomotion over terrain and says robots also need to navigate and understand where they are going, but it does not clearly distinguish crossing difficult terrain from deciding where the robot should go.

fable-5.1.text:
I think "solved" is a word I'd be careful with, because it depends a lot on what you actually mean by it. If the question is whether a legged robot can walk over stairs, rubble, a forest trail, using cameras or depth sensors as input, then yes, I'd say we're pretty far along. That's something that works reliably now in a lot of settings, and it's gone from research demo to something you can buy as a product in a surprisingly short time. A few years ago, blind locomotion was already pretty robust, and then adding perception on top of that, mostly through simulation and learning-based pipelines, really closed the gap for a lot of practical terrains.

But I think the honest answer is that it's solved for the terrains we've thought to put in simulation. The pipeline we and others use is essentially: build a terrain generator, train a policy with a lot of randomization, transfer it to the real robot. That works great as long as the world looks like what the simulator produces. Where it breaks is the long tail. Things like vegetation that looks like an obstacle but isn't, transparent or reflective surfaces, deformable ground, snow, a depth sensor that gets confused by sunlight. The robot doesn't fall because the controller is bad, it falls because its perception of the world was wrong and it had no way to know that.

So the way I think about it is that the low-level problem, mapping a reasonable representation of the terrain to foot placements and joint torques, is largely handled. What's not handled is the robustness of that representation, and the robot's ability to reason about uncertainty in it. Do I trust this height map? Should I slow down and probe this surface with my foot? Those are things humans and animals do constantly, and most current systems don't really do at all. They just commit.

And then there's the broader question of whether locomotion should even be treated as a separate problem anymore. Increasingly, what we want is a robot that moves through the world in service of some task, so navigation, manipulation, and locomotion start to blend together. Once you look at it that way, "walking is solved" becomes a bit of a narrow statement. The controller works, but integrating it into a system that makes good decisions about where to go and how to move is still very much open.

So my short answer would be: solved enough that it's no longer the interesting part for a lot of the research community, but not solved in the sense that you can deploy a robot anywhere and stop worrying about it.

r001.rationale: It describes locomotion as moving over terrain and contrasts that with the broader system deciding where to go and how to move.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by solved. If you mean, can we get a robot to use vision to walk over challenging terrain in a demonstration, then we can do quite a lot. But if you mean, can you put it in an unfamiliar environment and trust it to keep working reliably, I wouldn’t call that solved.

With vision, the robot has to connect what it sees to where it can safely step. Some of that is ambiguous: a surface might look solid but move when you put weight on it, or an obstacle might be partially hidden. So it needs to combine vision with feedback from contact and adapt when its expectations are wrong.

For me, the important question is less whether we can demonstrate a particular capability and more how broadly and reliably that capability works. There’s still a gap there.

r001.rationale: The response discusses walking over challenging terrain and reliability in unfamiliar environments, but it does not distinguish locomotion from navigation’s task of deciding where the robot should go.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by solved. If you mean, can we demonstrate a robot using vision to walk over some very challenging terrain, then yes, we can do that. But if you mean, can you put that robot in an arbitrary environment and trust it to keep working, I don’t think we’re there yet.

With vision, the robot has to deal with uncertainty in what it sees. It might miss an obstacle, or the terrain might look solid but move when you step on it. So it’s not just about planning where to put the feet. It’s also about reacting when the world is different from what you expected.

We’ve made a lot of progress, but there’s still a gap between an impressive demonstration and a system that works reliably every day. That reliability is where a lot of the interesting problems remain.

r001.rationale: The response discusses walking over challenging terrain and operating reliably in arbitrary environments, but it does not distinguish crossing terrain from deciding where the robot should go.
